headline: Trump ends his midterm pitch at the pool that peeled.
summary: Trump gives his closing midterm speech Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. In April he said he'd fix it in days for about $1.5 million. The work finished nearly three months late at more than ten times that, then algae bloomed and the blue liner peeled off. Trump blames vandals. His own US attorney blamed shoddy work.

cover_question.q: Why give the speech at that pool?

cover_answer: He says it'll show how beautiful it is.
table_question: When you mess something up, do you show it off or hide it?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The president is giving a speech today beside a long, flat pool in Washington. He had the pool fixed this year. It was supposed to take a few days and it took all summer, as long as your summer break, and then the water turned green. He says it looks beautiful now. The grown-ups are still arguing about that.
5-7.why: A pool that went green is a thing they can picture. The money and the blame can wait.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them a safe one: a long flat pool that was meant to take days, took all summer, and went green. The money and the blame stay with the grown-ups. Expect "is it fixed now?" Say the water is back in and the arguing is not over.

8-12.script: In April the president said he'd fix the Reflecting Pool in days for about $1.5 million. It finished nearly three months late at over ten times that, then algae bloomed and the blue liner peeled. Think of a bake sale plan: the guess, then the receipts. Today he's giving his last election speech there.
8-12.why: Guess, then receipts, is a comparison they can run.
8-12.why_long: This age checks whether adults apply rules to themselves, and this story is a comparison: the promise in April, days and $1.5 million, against the receipt, three months late at ten times the price. A bake sale budget is a plan they have blown. Expect "who broke it?" Vandals, says the president. Bad work, said his US attorney.

13-17.script: Why hold your closing speech at your most criticized project? Trump says it will show how beautiful the pool is. Second: he blames vandals, his ally Jeanine Pirro's office blamed shoddy work, and the one man charged was cleared. Does repeating a checked claim cost a politician anything?
13-17.why: Two accounts of one pool, side by side. Let them pick before you do.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the president says the pool was vandalized, and his own US attorney said it was shoddy work. The script puts both on the table and asks what repeating the first claim costs. Let them make the case either way before you grade it. Expect "does it matter for the election?" Nobody knows.

5-7.a: Sort of. It went green and the blue lining peeled. They drained it and fixed it again.

8-12.q: Why did it cost so much more?
8-12.a: The article doesn't say. His guess was $1.5 million; the bill was over ten times that.
Trump says vandals. The US attorney's office said bad work.

13-17.q: Why give the speech at that pool?
13-17.a: He says it'll show how beautiful it is. The AP calls it a break from his rallies.

13-17.q: Did the vandal story hold up?
13-17.a: No. Prosecutors dropped the one case and a judge dismissed it for good.
